Journal of Science Education and Technology (2024) 33:892–909 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-024-10131-x

## De‑mystifying the Influence of PhET Simulation on Engagement, Satisfaction, and Academic Achievement of Bhutanese Students in the Physics Classroom

**Tshering Dorji**[^1][ ** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0002-0022-6507) **Sumitra Subba**[^1][ ** ·**](http://orcid.org/0009-0006-4783-5752) **Tshering Zangmo2**[ ](http://orcid.org/0009-0003-9253-7314)

Accepted: 12 June 2024 / Published online: 26 June 2024 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2024

## Abstract This study employed a non-equivalent quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control-group design to study the effect of the PhET simulation intervention on students’ engagement, satisfaction, and academic achievement in the learning of direct current electric circuit concepts among Bhutanese students. We analysed the pre- and post-test scores and perceptions of 57 ninth-grade students, divided into experimental group (EG, _n_ = 29) and control group (CG, _n_ = 28), from one high school in Paro District, Bhutan_._ The EG students were taught with the PhET simulation intervention, while the CG students were taught with the traditional chalk- talk method. The pre- and post-test scores were collected with the Electric Circuits Conceptual Evaluation (ECEE) inventory. Mean, standard deviation, a two-sample _t_-test, and multiple linear regression (MLR) were computed using R and RStudio. The _t_-test revealed a statistically significant difference in the mean post-test scores of CG and EG students. MLR analysis further confirmed that this difference was due to the PhET simulation intervention, ruling out the influence of other confounding vari- ables. Additionally, an instrument called the PhET Engagement-Satisfaction Questionnaire was developed to assess EG students’ engagement level and satisfaction with the PhET simulation intervention. Confirmatory factor analysis and Cronbach’s alpha calculation confirmed its validity and reliability. Data from  the PhET Engagement-Satisfaction Questionnaire unveiled significant impact of the PhET simulation intervention on students’ engagement level and their overall satisfaction, reinforcing prior research. However, further research with a larger sample size, incorporating lesson observations, interviews, and our measurement tool, is necessary to ascertain whether the findings it yields align with the present study’s findings.

**Keywords** PhET simulations · Confirmatory factor analysis · Engagement · Satisfaction · RStudio

## Theoretical Framework and Hypothesis Development

This study is guided by several educational theories and models such as constructivist pedagogy, experiential learning theory, and technology acceptance model (TAM). Constructivist pedagogy and experiential learning theory, rooted in the constructivist learning theory, pioneered by Jean Piaget and Lev Vygotsky, emphasise active, contex- tual, and social learning, where learners construct knowl- edge through experiences and interactions with their envi- ronment (Richardson, 2003). Piaget’s theory emphasises the active role of learner in the learning process, suggest- ing that knowledge is best acquired through active interac- tion and hands-on activities rather than passively receiving and memorising information (Zajda, 2021). PhET simula- tion-assisted teaching supports this by providing interac- tive, hands-on experiences that engage students in active learning. For example, in the “Circuit Construction Kit” simulation used in this study, students can build their own electrical circuits by dragging and dropping components like batteries, wires, and light bulbs. They can change the configuration and immediately see the effects, such as how altering the resistance impacts the brightness of the light bulb. This hands-on activity requires students to actively engage with the concepts of electricity and electric cir- cuits. Additionally, the feedback provided by the PhET simulations to students while exploring the simulations resembles the concept of scaffolding proposed by Lev Vygotsky. Similar to how scaffolding, typically provided by a more knowledgeable other such as teacher or peer, assists learners in mastering tasks beyond their current level of competence, feedback mechanisms within PhET simulations serve to guide students through the learning process. For example, dragging a slider might change a variable, and the immediate feedback (in the form of vis- ual changes, numerical updates, or other indicators) helps users understand the relationship between their actions and the outcomes. PhET simulations also facilitate social interaction, another critical aspect of Vygotsky’s social constructivist theory, by encouraging collaborative prob- lem-solving and discussions among students. Addition- ally, to maximise the effectiveness of simulation-based teaching, Kolb’s (2014) experiential learning theory was also used. While direct research linking PhET simulations to Kolb’s experiential learning theory is lacking, Meyer et al.’s (2021) study in the clinical field suggests that inte- grating four stages of Kolb’s experiential learning theory into simulation-based education can significantly enhance 

students’ skills and performance across various subjects. Kolb proposed a four-stage learning cycle, which includes concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract con- ceptualisation, and active experimentation (Babin et al., [2019;](#conclusion-data-analysis-was-carried-out-by-zangmo-t-all-authors-discussed-the-results-approved-the-final-manuscript-as-submitted-and-agree-to-be) Lehane, 2020). According to Kolb, _concrete expe-_ _rience_ involves engaging in hands-on, discovery-based learning experiences like simulation, _reflective obser-_ _vation_ involves reflecting on their concrete experiences, _abstract conceptualisation_ involves conceptualising their observations to formulate hypotheses or mental models to explain the observed phenomena, and _active experimen-_ _tation_ involves testing their hypotheses through further experimentation (Babin et al., [2019;](#conclusion-data-analysis-was-carried-out-by-zangmo-t-all-authors-discussed-the-results-approved-the-final-manuscript-as-submitted-and-agree-to-be) Lehane, 2020). Even- tually, optimal learning takes place when learners experi- ence all four stages (Poore et al., 2014). Simulation-based teaching aligns well with this theory, as it offers opportu- nities for students to engage in immersive hands-on activi- ties, receive immediate feedback encouraging reflection, develop theories, and test those theories through further experimentation within the simulations. Furthermore, this study integrates technology acceptance model (TAM; Davis, 1987), into its theoretical framework. TAM pro- vides a framework for understanding whether users will accept or refuse a technology (Fussell & Truong, 2022). According to TAM, perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness are critical factors that influence users’ atti- tudes towards and acceptance of a new technology (Fussell & Truong, 2022). If users perceive a technology as easy to use, they are more likely to accept and adopt it, whereas perceived complexity or difficulty may deter it. Users are more likely to accept and use a technology if they believe it will be useful to them in achieving their goals. In the context of this study, TAM is used to explore how Bhuta- nese students perceive PhET simulations. We hypothesised that if students perceive the simulations as easy to use and useful for understanding scientific concepts, they are more likely to engage with the PhET simulations. This height- ened engagement, in turn, was anticipated to positively influence their learning outcomes.

## Method

### Research Design

This study used a mixed method approach. The study employed a non-equivalent quasi-experimental pre-test/ post-test control-group design to compare the academic per- formance of experimental group (EG) students, who were taught with the PhET simulation intervention, with those in the control group (CG), who were taught with the traditional chalk-talk method. The concepts covered in the study was direct current (DC) circuit concepts, including topics such 

### as electric current, resistance, potential difference, electric power, series, and parallel DC circuits. The Electric Circuits Conceptual Evaluation (ECEE) inventory was used as both pre- and post-test measures. To assess EG students’ engage- ment level and satisfaction with the PhET simulation inter- vention, data were collected through a self-created measure called the PhET Engagement-Satisfaction Questionnaire and a qualitative, open-ended reflective survey.

### Setting, Sample Size, and Sampling Method

This study employed a two-sample approach. Initially, data was collected from 302 tenth–twelfth grade students from two higher secondary schools in western Bhutan to assess the questionnaire’s psychometric properties. This sample was 59.9% male and 40.1% female, with an average age of 16.2 years. Subsequently, for the pri- mary research investigation, akin to a second pilot study due to the small sample size, 57 ninth-grade students enrolled in three different sections at our school were used. This sample, with an average age of 15.6, was used to address the research questions. This smaller sample consisted of 57.9% males and 42.1% females. These students were divided into two groups: CG (_n_ = 28) 

**Table 2** CFA results of PhET Engagement-Satisfaction Questionnaire

and EG (_n_ = 29). To ensure impartial group labelling, a flip of the coin was conducted. Both sets of samples were selected via the convenience sampling method. This approach was chosen for its practicality and ease of access to the student population under investigation (Andrade, [2021)](#conclusion-data-analysis-was-carried-out-by-zangmo-t-all-authors-discussed-the-results-approved-the-final-manuscript-as-submitted-and-agree-to-be).

## Instruments

**ECEE**

We used the original English version of the ECEE, a con- cept inventory developed by Sokoloff (1992), to assess students’ mastery of direct current (DC) circuit concepts, including electric current, resistance, potential difference, electric power, series, and parallel DC circuits. Permission to download and use the ECEE inventory from [https:// www. physp ort. org ](https://www.physport.org)was approved. The original ECEE contained 45 multiple-choice test items. However, only 32 items, specifi- cally items 1 to 16 and 23 to 38, pertaining to DC electric circuit concepts, were included in this study. The developer, Sokoloff (1992), carried out a rigorous process to establish its validity and reliability.

**PhET Engagement‑Satisfaction Questionnaire**

### A tool named PhET Engagement-Satisfaction Questionnaire (Table [2)](#as-electric-current-resistance-potential-difference-electric-power-series-and-parallel-dc-circuits-the-electric-circuits-conceptual-evaluation-ecee-inventory-was-used-as-both-pre--and-post-test-measures-to-assess-eg-students-engage--ment-level-and-satisfaction-with-the-phet-simulation-inter--vention-data-were-collected-through-a-self-created-measure-called-the-phet-engagement-satisfaction-questionnaire-and-a-qualitative-open-ended-reflective-survey) was developed to estimate students’ engagement level and satisfaction with the PhET simulation intervention during their study of DC electric circuit concepts. A total of 21 observed variables (items) were adapted from existing sur- vey questionnaires (Jefferies & Rizzolo, 2006; Lindgren et al., 2016) and the TAM model. The questionnaire consisted of three sections. Section A collected participants’ demographic information, such as their current grade level, age, and other confounding variables (discussed below). Sections B and C with, 11 and 10 items, respectively, measured EG students’ engagement level and satisfaction with the PhET simulation intervention. Each item was measured on a five-point Likert- type scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 2 = Disagree, 3 = Neutral, 4 = Agree, and 5 = Strongly Agree). Negatively keyed items were reverse-scored before conducting any analysis. Before administering the PhET Engagement-Satisfaction Questionnaire to the actual sample, a pilot study was con- ducted to assess its psychometric properties via CFA and Cronbach’s alpha analysis. The details are mentioned under the “Statistical Analysis” section.

**Confounding Variables**

Researchers (e.g. Pourhoseingholi et al., 2012; Theobald & Freeman, 2014) have asserted that failure to control the impacts of confounding variables in a non-equivalent quasi- experimental pre-test/post-test control-group research design study can potentially mislead researchers and lead to valid- ity issues. Confounding variables refer to the extraneous variables that have the potential to exert an influence on the response variable (Pourhoseingholi et al., 2012). There- fore, to confirm whether the difference in the mean post- test scores of the CG and EG students is due to the PhET simulation intervention, we collected data on students’ prior exposure to PhET simulation, hours spent preparing for the post-test, prior knowledge of taught concepts, and level of motivation to learn physics.

### Qualitative Reflective Survey

To elicit a comprehensive understanding of students’ percep- tions regarding the usefulness of PhET simulation interven- tion, we also collected qualitative reflective responses from a few EG students using open-ended questions. Students responded to the reflective survey in English.

### Data Collection Procedures and Intervention

This study was conducted during the academic year 2023. Ethical approval for conducting the study was sought from 

the school’s principal. The study’ purpose and objectives were thoroughly explained to the school principal and participants. Informed consent was obtained from all parents and partici- pants, given the students’ minor status. Prior to the instruc- tional intervention, a pre-test was administered to diagnose and evaluate students’ prior knowledge of DC electric circuits. This pre-test also served to determine whether the academic achievement levels of the CG and EG students were similar before the intervention (Banda & Nzabahimana,[ 2022)](#conclusion-data-analysis-was-carried-out-by-zangmo-t-all-authors-discussed-the-results-approved-the-final-manuscript-as-submitted-and-agree-to-be). Subse- quently, as mentioned earlier, the CG students were then taught in a traditional way with the chalk-talk method, while the EG students were taught with a free-ware PhET simulation titled “Circuit Construction Kit: DC” (available at [https:// phet. color ado. edu)](https://phet.colorado.edu). To minimise any teacher-related effects, both groups were taught by the same teacher in English, who was one of the researchers. The CG students did not use both real circuits or PhET simulations during the study. They only engaged in theoretical learning and traditional problem-solving exercises (network problem-solving) without hands-on practice, either with simulations or physical components. As for the EG stu- dents, they participated in both hands-on practice with real circuit and PhET simulation activities (see Fig. 8). Initially, they engaged in PhET simulation activities. After mastering the concepts through simulation, they transitioned to practical work with real circuits. They used battery eliminators (device that provide a stable DC power supply by converting AC from the mains), wires, resistors, ammeters, one-way keys, voltme- ters, and multimeters (see Fig. 8), to recreate the circuits they had built virtually. This practical work involved constructing series and parallel circuits, measurement of actual current and voltage, and observation of any disparities between simulated and real circuit behaviour. Both activities were conducted in English, as it serves as the medium of instruction in Bhutan’s modern educational system (Dendup, 2023).

To develop the PhET simulation activities for EG students, we used six heuristics—a research-based strategies devel- oped by Rehn et al. (2013)—to facilitate the productive use of the PhET simulations. Table [1 ](#positive-impact-of-phet-simulation-interventions-on-the-in-bhutan-specifically-this-study-addressed-the-following-academic-performance-of-students-in-addition-to-academic-research-questions)depicts these six heuristics and describes their implementation in the present study. After the interventions, a post-intervention post-test was administered to both classes. Then, EG students’ engagement and satisfaction levels with the PhET simu- lation intervention were assessed using the PhET Engage- ment-Satisfaction Questionnaire and a qualitative, open- ended reflective survey. Students completed their ECEE pre- and post-tests using the English version, the only version available, and also responded to the two survey questionnaires in English.

**Statistical Analysis**

Data was entered into Microsoft Excel, cleaned, and analysed using the statistical software RStudio, version 

2024.04.1 + 748, as explained below. Statistical analysis was considered significant at the _p_ \< 0.05 level.

**PhET Engagement‑Satisfaction Questionnaire’s Psychometric Evaluation**

CFA was conducted with initial data collected from 302 students to assess its structural or factorial validity (i.e. whether 21 items are related to the two hypothesised latent variables (factors), engagement and satisfaction, as expected) of the PhET Engagement-Satisfaction Ques- tionnaire. CFA was chosen because of its unique ability to explore the causal relationships among latent and observed variables in pre-defined, theory-derived models (Tavakol & Wetzel, 2020). CFA was conducted using the cfa () func- tion from the lavaan package in R (Rosseel, 2012). Before conducting CFA, data screening procedures were con- ducted, including the examination of missing data, outli- ers, and univariate and multivariate normality. Fortunately, there were no missing data or outliers in our datasets. The univariate and multivariate normalities of the data were checked using the mardia () function from the _mvnormal-_ _Test_ package (Zhou & Shao, 2014). Since our data did not meet both the univariate and multivariate normality assumptions (Li, 2016), we chose Diagonally Weighted Least Square (DWLS) for estimating CFA models (Ross & Bauldry, 2022). We set the variance of the latent vari- able to one. To assess the CFA model’s goodness-of-fit, various goodness-of-fit indices including chi-square test (_χ_2) and _χ_2/_df_, Root Mean Square Error of Approxima- tion (RMSEA) with 95% confidence interval (CI), Com- parative Fit Index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), and Standardised Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR) were used. The CFA model was deemed to be a good fit for the data when the _χ_2 result was non-significant (Marsh & Hocevar, 1985) and the _χ_2/_df_ \< 2 (Hu & Bentler, 1999; Schreiber et al., 2006). The adequacy of the other fit indi- ces was assessed by comparing them to the threshold val- ues recommended in prior research studies (Hu & Bentler, 1999; Ross & Bauldry, 2022; Schreiber et al., 2006); RMSEA ≤ 0.05, CFI ≥ 0.95, and SRMR \< 0.08 indicate the model’s good fit to the observed data. Due to the _χ_2 statistic’s sensitivity to the sample size (Marsh & Hocevar, 1985) and departures from multivariate normality in the data (Ross & Bauldry, 2022), more importance is placed on these fit indices, because the _χ_2 statistic tends to reject the null hypothesis in samples larger than 100 (Lebowitz et al., 2019; Ross & Bauldry, 2022). Finally, we used the semPlot () function from the _semPlot_ package to visualise the ultimate CFA model (Fig. [1)](#result). Furthermore, to estimate the questionnaire’s construct reliability, Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was calculated and assessed following George and Mallery’s (2019) guidelines.

### Main Data Analysis

To address research question 1, tables, graphs, mean (_M_), median, standard deviations (_SD_), and interquartile range (IQR) were used to describe and summarise the pre- and post-test scores collected from EG and CG students. Addi- tionally, an independent two-sample _t_-test (hereafter _t_-test) was computed to examine the statistical significance of the difference in means of the pre- and post-test scores of CG and EG students. To quantify the magnitude of the dif- ference, if any, Cohen’s _d_ effects size was calculated. Its magnitude was assessed using the thresholds outlined in Cohen (1992), that is, \|_d_\|\< 0.2 “negligible”, \|_d_\|\< 0.5 “small”, \|_d_\|\< 0.8 “medium”, otherwise “large”. Assumptions of the _t_-test were checked, including the normality of the data and Levene’s test of homogeneity of variances. No violations were observed. Specifically, the normality of the data was checked visually by plotting diagnostic plots such as histo- grams and Quantile–Quantile plots (Q-Q plot). Additionally, the Shapiro–Wilk test, skewness, and kurtosis values were also computed.

Parametric tests, like _t_-tests, assume the data follows a normal distribution and that the variances of two groups (EG and CG) are equal. The Shapiro–Wilk test assesses if the data are normally distributed, while Levene’s test checks whether the variances of two groups are equal. If both tests’ _p_ values are greater than the chosen significance level ( = 0.05), it indicates the data follows a normal distribution and variances are similar between groups. Skewness and kurtosis also help assess the normality of the data. Skewness measures the asymmetry of a distribution, with a skewness of zero indicating symmetry (Kallner, 2018). Kurtosis measures the peakedness or tailedness of the distribution, with a kurtosis of 3 indicating a normal distribution (Kallner, 2018). Deviations from these values result in the non-normality of the data. In such cases, non-parametric tests may be more suitable (Mishra et al., 2019). Histograms and Q-Q plots provide a graphical representation of data distributions. Additionally, means and SD were calculated for each item under the engagement and satisfaction constructs. The means were categorised into three levels: low (1.7 or lower), medium (1.8–3.5), and high (3.6–5.0) to describe EG students’ level of engagement and satisfaction with the PhET simulation intervention. Furthermore, Pearson’s correlation coefficient was calculated to examine the potential association between engagement, satisfaction, and the post-test scores achieved by EG students. Finally, qualitative analysis was performed on the data obtained from the post-intervention reflective survey to gain comprehensive understanding of students’ percep- tions about the PhET simulation intervention. To address research question 2, MLR analysis was con- ducted. This analytical approach enabled us to thoroughly examine whether the post-test score gains of EG students 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1** Ultimate CFA model. Items E7 and E9 were excluded due to factor loadings below 0.40

were due to the PhET simulation intervention or other con- founding variables (Banda & Nzabahimana, [2022;](#conclusion-data-analysis-was-carried-out-by-zangmo-t-all-authors-discussed-the-results-approved-the-final-manuscript-as-submitted-and-agree-to-be) Theobald & Freeman, 2014). We defined and integrated the follow- ing confounders into our MLR analysis: Pre\_Test (students’ pre-test scores), Post\_Test (students’ post-test scores), Treat- ment (whether students were in the class that received PhET simulation intervention; Treatment = 1 if the students were in intervention class and a 0 otherwise), Prior\_Exposure\_ PhET (how frequently students have used PhET simulation before the current study; Prior\_Exposure\_PhET = 0 if they have never used, 1 if they have used it a couple of times, 2 if they have used it few times a week and 3 if they have used it daily), Hours\_Spent (hours spent preparing for post- test; Hours\_Spent = 1 if less than one hour, 2 if 1–2 h, 3 if 3–4 h, 4 if 5–6 h and 5 if more than 6 h), Prior\_Knowl- edge (students’ prior knowledge of DC electric circuit on a scale of 1–5; 1 = very weak foundation and 5 = very strong foundation), and Motivation (students’ level of motivation to learn Physics on scale of 1–5). The regression model was specified as Post\_Test = _β_0 + _β_[^1] (Pre\_Test) + _β_2 (Treat- ment) + _β_3 (Prior\_Exposure\_PhET) + _β_4 (Hours\_Spent) + _β_5 (Prior\_Knowledge) + _β_6 (Motivation) + . Here, _β_0, _β_[^1], _β_2, _β_3, _β_4, _β_5, and _β_6 are the regression coefficients that describe 

the relationship between each confounder and the students’ post-test scores and represent the random disturbance or error (Chatterjee & Hadi, 2013). Assumptions of MLR were checked, including linearity, normality of residuals, and homoscedasticity. No violations were observed.

## Result

**PhET Engagement‑Satisfaction Questionnaire’s Psychometric Properties**

The initial CFA with initial data indicated an accept- able fit of the data to the hypothesised two-factor meas- urement model with 21 observed variables (_χ_2 (188, _N_ = 302) = 253.733, _p_ = 0.001, _χ_2/_df_ = 1.35, CFI = 0.991, TLI = 0.990, RMSEA = 0.034 (90% CI \[0.022, 0.044\], _p_ = 0.996), and SRMR = 0.063), providing evidence for the questionnaire’s factorial validity. The standardised loadings for each observed variable on their respective latent factors ranged from 0.210 to 0.727 (Table [2)](#as-electric-current-resistance-potential-difference-electric-power-series-and-parallel-dc-circuits-the-electric-circuits-conceptual-evaluation-ecee-inventory-was-used-as-both-pre--and-post-test-measures-to-assess-eg-students-engage--ment-level-and-satisfaction-with-the-phet-simulation-inter--vention-data-were-collected-through-a-self-created-measure-called-the-phet-engagement-satisfaction-questionnaire-and-a-qualitative-open-ended-reflective-survey). While this model’s fit indices are reasonably good, item-level inspection revealed some items factor loading below 0.400. Although there is no

universally accepted cut-off value for factor loadings (Doll et al., 1995), following Ross and Bauldry’s (2022) recom- mendation, we dropped items E7 and E9 under engage- ment factor with factor loadings below 0.40 and re-ran the CFA. The respecified model, represented by Fig. [1,](#result) yielded an even better fit (_χ_2 (151, _N_ = 302) = 170.559, _p_ = 0.132, _χ_2/_df_ = 1.13, CFI = 0.997, TLI = 0.997, RMSEA = 0.021 (90% CI \[0.000, 0.035\], _p_ = 1.00), and SRMR = 0.056) with standardised factor loadings ranging from 0.452 to 0.722. All of the goodness-of-fit indices of the model comfortably met the threshold values recommended in prior works (Hu & Bentler, 1999; Ross & Bauldry, 2022), indicating a good fit between the model and the data. Hence, no further modifica- tion to the model was deemed necessary. The plot displayed in Fig. [1 ](#result)shows the ultimate CFA model with 19 measure- ment items. Items E7 and E9 under the engagement factor were excluded due to factor loadings below 0.400. In Fig. [1,](#result) a single-headed arrow from a latent to the observed variables shows the causal relationship between them, and a double-headed arrow shows a covariance between the factors (Li, 2016; Tavakol & Wetzel, 2020). The correlation between the engagement and satisfaction construct was 0.89. The little double-headed arrows out- side the observed variable boxes represent the error vari- ances, capturing unaccounted-for variability or measure- ment error within the 19 items. While collecting data from 302 students, we did not consider confounding variables, also known as extraneous variables, which may uniquely

The instrument’s construct reliability was evidenced by Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.92 (95% CI = 0.90–0.93). The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was 0.83 (95% CI = 0.79–0.85) for the engagement factor and 0.87 (95% CI = 0.85–0.90) for the satisfaction factor of the PhET Engagement-Satisfaction Questionnaire. These values indicate good to excellent internal consistency reliability (George & Mallery, 2019). Collectively, the CFA and Cron- bach’s alpha analysis support the validity and reliability of the 19-item PhET Engagement-Satisfaction Questionnaire.

The Pearson’s correlation coefficient unveiled a positive moderate correlation, _r _(27) = 0.48, _p_ = 0.00, between EG students’ engagement level and their post-test scores. Addi- tionally, this study found a moderate, positive correlation, _r _(27) = 0.43, _p_ = 0.02, between students’ satisfaction levels during the PhET simulation intervention and their post- test scores. Both correlations were statistically significant at the = 0.05 level. These results suggest that the PhET simulation intervention’s engagement and satisfaction had a moderate influence on students’ academic achievement in post-intervention assessment (Almasri, [2022)](#conclusion-data-analysis-was-carried-out-by-zangmo-t-all-authors-discussed-the-results-approved-the-final-manuscript-as-submitted-and-agree-to-be). Since stu- dents’ prior knowledge of the subject matter also contributed 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

to the improvement in the post-test scores (refer to the MLR result), participants, on average, did not strongly agree with item S16 under the satisfaction factor.

### Results for Question 2

The results of the MLR analysis are summarised in Table 7. The fitted regression equation was Post\_Test = 9.487 + 2.261 (Treatment) + 0.251 (Pre\_Test) − 0.152 (Prior\_ Exposure\_PhET) − 0.715 (Hours\_Spent) + 0.017 (Prior\_ Knowledge) + 0.191 (Motivation). The overall model was statistically significant: _F_(6, 50) = 9.586, _p_ = 5.231_e_ − 07, _R_2 = 0.535. The adjusted _R_2 value was 0.479 (47.9%), indicating a good model fit (Cronk, 2020).

The MLR analysis showed that the PhET simulation intervention had a significant positive effect on students’ post-test scores (  = 2.261, _p_ = _6_.17e − 08), even after con- trolling for all other confounders. This analysis revealed that, on average, for each additional point on the treatment scale, there is a statistically significant increase of 2.261 points in the post-test score (_p_ \< 0.05), indicating a robust and posi- tive relationship between the treatment and post-test scores. Additionally, the pre-test scores had a significant positive effect on students’ post-test scores (  = 0.251, _p_ = 0.001) after controlling for all other confounders. This analysis revealed that, on average, for each additional point acquired in the pre-test, there is a slight increase of 0.251 points in the post-test score. This relationship between the pre-test and post-test scores is statistically significant (_p_ \< 0.05). However, prior exposure to PhET (−0.152, _p_ = 0.552), hours spent preparing for the post-test (−0.715, _p_ = 0.130), prior knowledge of taught concepts (0.017, _p_ = 0.948), and level of motivation to learn physics (0.191, _p_ = 0.302) did not have a statistically significant effect on post-test scores (_p_ \> 0.05).

## Discussion

This study investigated the experiences of Bhutanese stu- dents as they engaged with the free-ware “Circuit Construc- tion Kit: DC” PhET simulation to learn DC electric circuit concepts (Fig. 8). Following our initial pilot study involv- ing 302 students, this research can be considered a second pilot study due to the smaller sample size of 57 participants. Despite this limitation, the results offer additional empirical validation for existing research, affirming the PhET simula- tions as a potent educational tool that enhances students’ engagement, satisfaction, and academic performance. From the post-test score analysis, we found that students in EG, who received PhET simulation intervention, per- formed better on average than their counterparts in the CG, who did not receive PhET simulation intervention. This is evident from the higher mean and median post-test scores 

of the EG students compared to the CG students (Table 4). Moreover, a _t_-test confirmed that the observed difference was not due to random chance but rather a consequence of the PhET simulation intervention (_p_ \< 0.05). The MLR analysis provided further confirmation that the gain in the post-test scores among the EG students was due to the PhET simulation intervention and students’ prior knowledge of the subject matter and not due to some other confounding vari- ables, including prior exposure to PhET, hours spent prepar- ing for the post-test, prior knowledge of taught concepts, and level of motivation to learn physics. Since students’ prior knowledge of the subject matter also contributed to the improvement in the post-test scores, participants, on aver- age, did not strongly agree with item S16 under the satisfac- tion factor. Nevertheless, the PhET simulation has positively influenced EG students’ scores in the post-intervention assessment. These results align with the findings of Banda and Nzabahimana ([2022)](#conclusion-data-analysis-was-carried-out-by-zangmo-t-all-authors-discussed-the-results-approved-the-final-manuscript-as-submitted-and-agree-to-be). Banda and Nzabahimana ([2022)](#conclusion-data-analysis-was-carried-out-by-zangmo-t-all-authors-discussed-the-results-approved-the-final-manuscript-as-submitted-and-agree-to-be) investigated the impact of PhET simulation on students’ motivation and academic achievement in learning oscilla- tions and waves among Malawian secondary students. The _t_-test showed a statistically significant difference between the EG and CG students’ mean post-test scores. Also, the results from linear regression indicated that the difference between the two groups in the post-test was due to the inter- vention and not owing to other students’ characteristics (Banda & Nzabahimana, [2022)](#conclusion-data-analysis-was-carried-out-by-zangmo-t-all-authors-discussed-the-results-approved-the-final-manuscript-as-submitted-and-agree-to-be).

Our study also unveiled the substantial influence of the PhET simulation on students’ levels of engagement and overall satisfaction with the learning experience. The quantitative results obtained from PhET Engagement- Satisfaction Questionnaire provided compelling evidence of the high level of engagement among students exposed to the PhET simulation intervention. As depicted in Table 5, the mean engagement score, measured on a five-point Likert scale, surpassed 3.8, categorising the students’ engagement level as “High”. This is also evident from the low mean score (_M_ = 1.7) on item E6 (_I found the PhET simulation-assisted learning boring and uninteresting_) under engagement construct. This data strongly supports the notion that PhET simulation is a great pedagogical tool to effectively captivate and involve students in the learning process. Additionally, qualitative feedback obtained from the reflective survey at the end of the instruction provided robust support for this quantitative finding. EG students expressed overwhelmingly positive feedback regarding their experience with the PhET simulation. They found the PhET simulation to be highly engaging and effective, providing an interactive, hands-on approach to experimenting with different circuit designs, observing the outcomes, and making quick modifications. Additionally, students appreciated the challenging yet engaging nature of the PhET simulation activities, which not only piqued their interest but also facilitated their active 

participation.
